summary:
MoonKeeper is a free 3D browser-based space survival game designed for students aged 7–18, combining real NASA science with interactive gameplay and educational challenges.

On the Moon, a devastating meteor shower has damaged every station. As the last survivor at Tranquility Deep, you must work alongside your robot companion, REGO, to survive until rescue arrives. Repair solar panels, maintain oxygen supplies, recycle water, grow food, extract ice, and rescue stranded astronauts while managing limited resources.

Every mission features interactive minigames inspired by real scientific and engineering procedures. Players also face realistic emergencies, including solar storms, moonquakes, and meteoroid impacts, using data from NASA's DONKI archive and Apollo missions.

MoonKeeper also introduces Mars Exploration, where players visit a 14-building research outpost on Arcadia Planitia, explore terrain based on NASA's MOLA elevation data, drive rovers, interact with crew members, and experience Martian dust storms.

Beyond entertainment, MoonKeeper teaches problem-solving, resource management, engineering, and space science through hands-on experiences. Teachers can incorporate the game into a 40-minute classroom lesson.

The game runs directly in any browser, requires no downloads or registration, and offers its lunar adventure in 16 languages, making space education accessible and engaging for young explorers worldwide.
details:
MoonKeeper — NASA Space Apps 2026

Project Details

What It Does

I created MoonKeeper, a 3D survival and building game that teaches players what it takes to keep a space station running on another world. My goal was to turn real space science and engineering challenges into an interactive experience where players learn by making decisions and solving problems.

The main adventure takes place on the Moon, at a station called Tranquility Deep, located inside a real lunar pit in the Sea of Tranquility (8.3355°N, 33.222°E), which scientists believe may connect to an underground lava tube.

The story begins after a meteor shower damages every station on the Moon. The player is a rookie astronaut and the only survivor at Tranquility Deep, accompanied by a small robot named REGO.

With rescue still days away, players must manage electricity, oxygen, water, and food while repairing damaged equipment and keeping the station operational.

I designed the game so that survival depends on the decisions players make. Every repair requires resources, every action takes time, and every mistake can have consequences.

New Feature: Mars Exploration (Preview)

I recently expanded MoonKeeper by introducing a second world: Mars.

The Mars preview takes place at a 14-building surface outpost on Arcadia Planitia (39.5°N, 191.2°E), an area where orbiters have detected evidence of water ice beneath the surface.

I used NASA's Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) data to create the planet map, the surrounding 192 km region, terrain slopes, and distant skyline.

For the immediate surface environment, I used observations from Martian landers as references while making some adjustments for gameplay.

I also wanted players to understand the difference between actual scientific observations and fictional design elements. Each building therefore includes a panel displaying its operational information and labels identifying whether the underlying concepts are observed, demonstrated, proposed, or created for the game.

In Mars exploration mode, players can drive a rover across a 1.6 km environment, discover eight locations, enter the Command Habitat, and interact with a crew of three astronauts.

I developed a system where the crew's responses depend on the station's current conditions. For example, switching off a building affects the base's resources, and the consequences become visible over the following hours.

I also added a dust storm simulation that demonstrates how Martian dust affects sunlight, shadows, and solar electricity generation.

To make the experience educational, I developed a Mars Science Center featuring six interactive demonstrations:

  1. Gravity on different worlds
  2. Atmospheric pressure
  3. Solar energy and dust storms
  4. Producing oxygen from the atmosphere
  5. Extracting water from ice
  6. Traveling between the Moon and Mars

Each demonstration includes scientific formulas and NASA references.

I also created an initial Mars survival mission involving dust storms, equipment failures, and repairs, where players can succeed or fail depending on their decisions.

How It Works

One of my main design decisions was to make the game hands-on rather than simply asking players to click buttons.

For example, when a solar panel breaks, players must physically remove it, transport it using the rover, bring it through the airlock, repair it at the Fix-It Bench, and reinstall it outside.

I designed each repair task as a short interactive minigame inspired by real engineering procedures.

These activities include tightening bolts to the correct torque, welding damaged surfaces, connecting electrical cables, safely switching circuit breakers, and testing whether a repaired compartment can maintain pressure.

I also built several connected survival systems.

Power Management

I created one central Power Board for the entire station. Increasing electricity for oxygen production means reducing the energy available for other equipment, such as heating or farm lighting.

During the approximately two-week lunar night, solar panels stop producing electricity, leaving players dependent on batteries and a small reactor.

Air Pressure and Station Damage

I designed each station room as a sealed compartment. If a room is damaged, air begins escaping. Players must repair the leak or seal off the room to protect the rest of the station.

Life Support

I implemented water recycling, oxygen production through water electrolysis, hydroponic food production, LED growing lights, egg production from hens, and ice extraction from a permanently shadowed crater.

Real NASA Events

I wanted the emergencies to be based on real historical events rather than completely random fictional disasters.

I incorporated 181 solar events recorded between 2011 and 2026 from NASA's DONKI archive.

I also used Apollo seismic records containing 28 shallow moonquakes and 213 meteoroid impacts.

Rescue and Exploration

Players can drive a rover or fly a rocket hopper to three other lunar stations to rescue astronauts and collect supplies.

However, rescuing additional people also increases the station's resource requirements. For example, I use a daily oxygen consumption value of approximately 0.84 kg per person.

My intention was to make every decision involve a trade-off.

Benefits and Intended Impact

My main goal with MoonKeeper is to make space science more accessible, especially to younger students.

I wanted children to understand the challenges of living beyond Earth through experience rather than memorizing scientific facts.

By completing a mission, I hope players can explain why surviving on the Moon is difficult and how engineers might address problems such as:

  • Long lunar days and nights
  • Vacuum and atmospheric pressure
  • Limited electricity
  • Water and oxygen recycling
  • Food production
  • Radiation protection
  • Underground habitats and natural rock shielding

Instead of presenting long scientific explanations before gameplay, I introduce concepts when players encounter problems that require them.

After each emergency, I include a short question to help reinforce what they learned.

I also developed a teacher resource page containing a 40-minute lesson plan, learning objectives, and a final reflection question.

I want MoonKeeper to be useful both as entertainment and as an educational classroom tool.

Who It Is For

I designed MoonKeeper primarily for students aged 7 to 18, with four gameplay modes for different experience levels.

Cadet Mode (Ages 7–10): A four-day mission with more guidance and simpler challenges.

Pilot Mode (Ages 11–14): A seven-day mission with increased responsibilities.

Commander Mode (Ages 15–18): A ten-day mission with more demanding resource management and limited materials.

Unlimited Mode: A creative building experience where players can develop their own lunar settlement.

To improve accessibility, I added a guidance system that highlights REGO's recommendations and displays a path on the floor.

REGO can also read instructions aloud using the device's built-in speech functionality.

I included adjustable text sizes, color-blind-friendly options, graphics settings, and mobile controls.

Tools and Programming Languages

I developed MoonKeeper using JavaScript (ES modules), HTML, CSS, and Three.js for the 3D environments.

I chose this approach because I wanted the game to be accessible directly through a browser without requiring downloads, accounts, or a separate installation.

The game is hosted on GitHub Pages, runs without a backend server, and saves player progress locally in the browser.

I also used Node.js scripts to download and process NASA datasets and run automated tests.

For example, I implemented simulation tests to check whether each survival mission can be completed successfully.

For visual content, I used Higgsfield to help generate 2D artwork, while Claude assisted me with programming, debugging, and parts of the scientific documentation.

I directed the overall game concept, designed the experience, and guided the development process.

What Makes My Project Creative

What makes MoonKeeper different is my decision to combine a survival game with a real, scientifically interesting lunar location and historical NASA event data.

Rather than inventing an entirely fictional environment, I placed the main station inside a real lunar pit that may lead to an unexplored lava tube.

I also used actual recorded solar storms, moonquakes, and meteoroid impacts to create emergencies.

This means players encounter events inspired by real scientific records, including historical dates.

Another important part of my design is that nothing comes without a cost.

When players increase oxygen production, they consume more electricity. When they rescue an astronaut, they must provide additional food, air, and water. When they repair a damaged station, they use time and materials that could have been spent elsewhere.

I believe this teaches an important lesson that applies beyond space exploration.

Resources are limited, and every decision has consequences.

My goal was to help players develop the habit of asking, "What will this decision cost, and what am I giving up?"

This is something I believe is just as valuable on Earth as it is in space.

Factors I Considered

Age and Learning Experience

I designed the interface around short instructions, clear objectives, and simple controls.

The main interaction key is E, which appears on screen when players need to perform an action.

I also made informational cards pause the game clock so younger students can read and understand instructions without feeling rushed.

Scientific Accuracy vs. Gameplay

I tried to use real scientific measurements wherever they meaningfully affect the experience.

However, I also recognize that some aspects of space exploration need to be simplified to create a playable game.

For example, I placed the ice mining location closer to the lunar station than actual polar ice deposits would be.

To make these differences transparent, I created a "Real or Made Up?" section explaining which features are scientifically supported and which were adjusted for gameplay.

Accessibility

I wanted MoonKeeper to run on ordinary school computers rather than requiring expensive gaming equipment.

I included graphics settings for less powerful devices and made the game accessible without registration, accounts, or tracking.

Visual Design

I wanted players to feel immersed in the experience without overwhelming the screen with unnecessary information.

For this reason, I kept most scientific citations and source notes outside the gameplay interface and organized them in the project's documentation.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

How I Used AI in My Project

I used AI tools throughout parts of MoonKeeper's development, but I want to clearly distinguish the work completed with AI assistance from the systems, designs, and decisions I directed myself.

1. Programming and Development — Claude

I used Claude by Anthropic as a coding assistant for JavaScript, HTML, CSS, automated testing, and data-processing scripts.

Claude helped me write and edit code based on my design instructions, identify and correct bugs, interpret test results, and organize some of the scientific and educational documentation.

I directed the game's overall concept, requirements, structure, and intended player experience.

To make this transparent, 75 commits in my GitHub repository include a "Co-Authored-By: Claude" acknowledgment.

2. Game Artwork — Higgsfield

I used Higgsfield's Marketing Studio image-generation models to create 111 pieces of 2D artwork.

These include comic illustrations, characters, event cards, room and station images, minigame backgrounds, title screens, and illustrations of Martian buildings, locations, and crew members.

I prepared written prompts to guide the visual generation.

Every AI-generated image displayed in the game includes a visible "SI-generated" label.

I also preserved the prompts in the repository under tools/art_jobs*.json.

3. Demo Video — Higgsfield and Gameplay Recordings

I used Higgsfield Seedance 2.5 for selected parts of my promotional video.

Specifically, I animated the title artwork for the opening shot and used video editing to adjust the lighting of one gameplay recording featuring the rocket hopper.

The original gameplay content of that shot was not changed.

I used a Higgsfield-generated illustration for the Mars title card and the game's existing artwork for the ending.

The other ten shots were recorded directly from actual gameplay.

I also added an "SI-generated" watermark to the demo video and disclosed the AI assistance in its description and file metadata.

4. Translations — Claude

I used Claude to translate the game into 15 additional languages, making the lunar adventure available in 16 languages.

I checked the translations using automated methods, although they have not yet been reviewed by native speakers.

I want to be transparent about this limitation.

5. Parts I Created Without Generative AI

Not every part of MoonKeeper was generated using AI.

I built the 3D environments, vehicles, robots, and characters using code-generated geometry and textures.

I also generated the game's music and sound effects through code.

For the promotional video, I synthesized the music using FFmpeg and simple audio tones.

The demo does not use a generated voice-over; I communicate the story through captions.

REGO's spoken dialogue uses the built-in speech synthesis of the player's device rather than an AI-generated voice service.

For Earth and Moon textures, I used NASA imagery.

6. Transparency and Scientific Attribution

I documented my AI use in the repository README and in a machine-readable disclosure file:

https://ruibinray.github.io/NASA-MoonKeeper/si-use.json

I also avoided using official NASA logos, insignia, flags, or mission identifiers in generated media.

Although I used NASA scientific resources, MoonKeeper is an independent educational project, not an official NASA product.

My purpose in using AI was to help turn my ideas into a playable experience while maintaining transparency about the tools involved.

Ultimately, MoonKeeper represents my effort to combine scientific research, game development, creative storytelling, and AI-assisted technology into an educational experience that makes learning about space exploration more interactive and accessible.
